name: Inversion table

card.summary: A tilting frame for hanging upside down, used for back traction and by height-curious forum users; any height change is described as temporary and reports of serious injury exist.
card.note: Case reports describe spinal cord injury and retinal detachment; contraindicated in several conditions.

quick.overview:
An inversion table is a frame that secures the legs and tilts the user toward or fully upside down. It is sold for back pain relief through spinal traction, and some looksmax.org users discuss it for 'heightmaxxing'.

Forum posters describe any gain as morning height that returns during the day, and some propose pairing it with glucosamine to keep it. No published trial of it for increasing adult height was found; reviews of inversion therapy describe benefits for back pain as short-term.
quick.mechanism: Body weight in the inverted position is said to create a distraction force that slightly and temporarily widens the spaces between vertebrae, similar in principle to clinical traction. Studies in healthy volunteers have measured effects of tilting on swallowing pressures, blood flow and intracranial pressure.
quick.risks: Case reports describe cervical spinal cord injury after falls from inversion tables, bilateral retinal detachment, and subdural hematomas in a person with a clotting disorder. Reference sources list heart disease, high blood pressure, glaucoma and pregnancy among conditions with higher risk, and recommend short sessions.

lead: An inversion table is a frame that secures the user's ankles or legs and tilts the body partly or fully upside down. It belongs to inversion therapy, a form of spinal traction in which body weight acts as a gentle pulling force on the spine; gravity boots, which hook onto a pull-up bar or doorway frame, are the other common device.[1] People use inversion tables mainly for back-pain relief and stretching, and in looksmaxxing circles some use them in the hope of getting a taller-looking, straighter and more decompressed posture, or of banking extra 'morning height'.[2][3]

Proponents say that hanging inverted creates a distractive force that slightly and temporarily increases the spacing between vertebrae, which may reduce pressure on nerve roots and help muscles relax.[1] Radiographic studies from the 1980s measured exactly this kind of separation in the lumbar spine during inversion.[4][5] Wikipedia reports that the main benefit is short-term, that it usually feels pleasant within minutes, and that sessions should be brief.[1]

Research on inversion has concentrated on back pain, on the physiology of being upside down, and on injuries. A small randomized pilot trial in patients with lumbar disc disease, case reports of serious injury, and studies of eye pressure and blood pressure during inversion make up most of the published literature.[6][7][8][9] No trial of inversion for increasing adult height was found, and on looksmax.org posters describe any height change as a morning effect that returns during the day.[2][3]
infobox: Raised eye pressure and blood pressure; falls; retinal detachment[8][10][12]
FDA regulates only when medical claims are made; many tables exempt[11]

paras: Inversion tables use ankle clamps or straps to hold the legs while a frame pivots the user backwards, so that the head sits below the feet at an adjustable angle from a slight tilt to near-vertical.[1] Gravity boots are ankle supports that hook onto an overhead bar or doorway frame, and some users add inverted crunches or squats to their workouts.[1] Wikipedia dates popular attention to a 1983 Time magazine feature titled 'Hang Ten'.[1]
Inversion is a form of passive traction. Clinical spinal traction in physiotherapy uses mechanical pull to the same end, and inversion substitutes the user's own body weight for the machine.[1][5]

The proposed mechanism is a distractive force on the spine that slightly and temporarily increases intervertebral spacing, which may reduce pressure on nerve roots and promote muscle relaxation.[1] Mayo Clinic's Edward Laskowski, cited on Wikipedia, says traction may reduce muscle spasm, rehydrate discs, reduce disc bulging and ease pain.[1]

For appearance, the chain that proponents describe is indirect: a decompressed spine and relaxed back muscles, possibly a slightly taller measured height after a session, and improved posture from more mobility and less stiffness. A looksmax.org thread cites one person who reportedly gained about two inches of morning height after ten days of inversion, with the gain fading by evening; the poster asked whether glucosamine sulphate might preserve it.[2] A reply there called the loss of height through the day a 'cope', and another thread's reply described inversion as only decompressing the spine.[2][3]
No studies found of inversion tables for increasing adult height. Studies exist of inversion for the spine, back pain and body physiology.

Spinal separation. In 1985, Kane and colleagues fully inverted 15 healthy men for 10 minutes and compared lateral X-rays taken before and after; inversion significantly increased separation at the front and back of the vertebral margins and within the intervertebral foramina, with most lumbar levels showing gains in at least one measure.[4] The same year, Gianakopoulos and colleagues tested three gravity-traction devices in 20 people with long-term low back pain and measured distraction of the lower lumbar spaces in every case; back symptoms improved in 13 of the 16 symptomatic patients, and the authors recommended medical supervision because of side effects.[5]

Back pain. A single-centre pilot randomized trial in Newcastle, UK, of 24 patients awaiting lumbar disc surgery compared physiotherapy alone with physiotherapy plus intermittent inversion traction. At 6 weeks, surgery was avoided in 10 of 13 patients in the inversion group and in 2 of 11 in the control group; the groups did not differ significantly on disability, pain, quality of life or MRI measures, and the authors called for a larger multicentre trial.[6]

Muscle activity. In a 2016 study, 60 healthy men were assigned to three traction-angle groups for six minutes of inversion traction; muscle activity of the lumbar erector spinae increased after traction, which the authors took to mean that inversion traction was more likely to raise muscle tension than to relax these muscles.[7]

Eye, blood pressure and cerebral effects. A 1983 study examined gravity inversion and systemic blood pressure, intraocular pressure and central retinal arterial pressure.[13] In 26 healthy young adults hung by the ankles, eye pressure averaged about 16 mm Hg standing and roughly 31 to 34 mm Hg inverted, with blood pressure rising from about 110/77 to 130/90 mm Hg, and both returned near baseline on standing.[8] The 1985 Gianakopoulos study also found inversion raised blood pressure and lowered heart rate.[5] A later ultrasound study measured optic nerve sheath diameter, heart rate, blood pressure and cerebral blood flow during table tilt.[14] Other small studies in volunteers examined pharyngeal swallowing pressures in ten healthy adults at several tilt angles and tibial bone microvascular flow in 18 volunteers during head-down tilt.[15][16]

Wikipedia lists heart disease, high blood pressure, eye diseases such as glaucoma, and pregnancy as conditions with higher risk, and notes that inversion increases heart rate and output, peripheral resistance and venous return.[1] Acid reflux in the inverted position can be painful and potentially dangerous, many people find the ankles uncomfortable after a few minutes, and new users sometimes need help getting out of the apparatus.[1] The 1985 Gianakopoulos study reported eye and throat petechiae, headaches, blurred vision and contact lens discomfort as side effects.[5]

A 2023 article in Disability and Rehabilitation, 'Recommendations for inversion table therapy', states that FDA device reports link these tables to serious injuries including spinal cord injury, fractures, lacerations and deaths, and that the FDA regulates them only when manufacturers make medical claims, which most do not, leaving many exempt.[11]

Published case reports include three cases of cervical spinal cord injury from falls from inversion tables, a further case of central cord syndrome after such a fall, bilateral retinal detachments associated with inversion therapy, and bilateral subdural hematomas in an adult with hereditary factor VII deficiency in which inversion and sit-ups were considered possible contributors.[9][10][12][17] A case report of spontaneous pneumomediastinum and subcutaneous emphysema following inversion maneuvers has also been published.[18]

On looksmax.org, inversion tables appear in height-focused threads. Some users report morning height gains and ask about cheap tables as a low-cost experiment, while others ask directly whether inversion is a 'cope' or increases height.[2][3] The recurring idea is that the gain is spinal decompression, visible when measuring in the morning, and that the question is whether it can be made to last.[2][3] Combinations with supplements such as glucosamine are proposed in the forum, and no study of that pairing was found.[2]

Related approaches include hanging from a pull-up bar, decompression stretches, yoga inversions, clinical spinal traction in physiotherapy and posture work. Inversion tables have also been used in a clinical setting alongside other treatments, for example in a Chinese surgical study of lower-pole renal stones and a case report of a non-pharmacological pain management approach in severe lumbar degeneration.[19][20]

timeline.event: Time magazine's 'Hang Ten' feature popularises gravity boots, as cited by Wikipedia; the same year Klatz and colleagues study the effects of gravity inversion on blood pressure and eye pressure.[1][13]
LeMarr, Golding and Adler report intraocular pressure roughly doubling in 26 healthy adults suspended inverted.[8]
Kane and colleagues publish X-ray evidence of lumbar separation during inversion; Gianakopoulos and colleagues report lumbar distraction with inversion devices.[4][5]
Heng and colleagues publish 'Changes in cardiovascular function during inversion' in the International Journal of Sports Medicine, cited on Wikipedia for cardiac concerns.[1]
Case report of bilateral subdural hematomas in an adult with factor VII deficiency, with inversion and sit-ups as possible contributors.[17]
Newcastle pilot randomized trial of inversion traction in patients with lumbar disc disease.[6]
Kim and Kang report increased lumbar erector spinae activity after inversion traction in 60 healthy men.[7]
Case report of bilateral retinal detachments associated with inversion table therapy.[12]
Three case reports of cervical spinal cord injury after falls from inversion tables.[9]
Kassay, Soliman and Jhawar review FDA device reports and the regulatory framework for inversion tables.[11]
Case report of central cord syndrome after a fall from an inversion table.[10]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, inversion tables come up in height-focused threads, where some users report morning height gains and others regard them as temporary.[2][3]

claims.claim: Using an inversion table can add inches of height.
claims.believers: A poster described someone reportedly going from 5'10 to 6'0 after ten days of inversion, though only in morning height, and said they were considering buying a cheap table to try it.[2]
claims.experts: Radiographic studies show temporary lumbar separation during inversion, and Wikipedia describes mainly short-term benefit.[1][4] No published trial has tested inversion for permanent height increase.

claims.claim: Glucosamine could lock in the height gained from inversion.
claims.believers: A poster proposed that glucosamine sulphate would 'keep the morning height gains' and that months of use might add up.[2]
claims.experts: No published studies were found testing glucosamine combined with inversion for height.

claims.claim: Inversion relaxes and decompresses the back.
claims.believers: Proponents describe hanging as relieving pressure on the spine, and Wikipedia cites traction advocates saying it may rehydrate discs and ease spasm.[1]
claims.experts: A small pilot trial found fewer surgeries in the inversion group without differences in pain or disability scores, and a 2016 study found increased erector spinae activity after inversion traction.[6][7]

claims.claim: Inversion is safe for everyone to try.
claims.believers: Forum threads treat buying a cheap table as a low-stakes experiment.[2]
claims.experts: Case reports describe spinal cord injury, retinal detachment and subdural hematoma; eye pressure roughly doubled in a study of inverted volunteers; and Wikipedia lists contraindications including heart disease, hypertension, glaucoma and pregnancy.[1][8][9][12][17]

claims.claim: Inversion gains vanish by evening, so they do not count.
claims.believers: Replies in forum threads call the daily loss a 'cope' and describe inversion as only decompressing the spine.[2][3]
claims.experts: The research literature measures spinal separation immediately before and after sessions and does not follow height across days or weeks.[4][5]

angle.text: Users hang inverted to decompress the spine, which proponents say lengthens the trunk slightly and temporarily and eases back stiffness. Forum posters describe any gain in height as showing up in the morning and fading through the day, and some look for ways to hold it.
